sheets.title: You may already have this covered
sheets.headline:
You may have tested the price.
Has anyone read the agreement?

blocks.text: Your filing gives us enough to see where the questions are. It does not tell us whether the economics you have are the ones available to you today.

blocks.label: Why a second look
paras: A bid can test price. A broker can test one market. Your buyers can run a strong process. None of them necessarily reads the agreement underneath the spend — the term, the fees, the minimums, the usage bands, the renewal mechanics, and what is actually being billed against what was agreed.
That is where a category specialist earns the hour.

columns.text: If the arrangement is already strong
We will tell you so, and you keep it — with something you did not have before: an independent read you can stand behind.
You see the options before anything changes, and you decide whether to act.

items: Read your FY2024 Form 990, line by line.
Read Part VII Section B, where your filing names three of your suppliers.
Compared each line against filers of your type.
Checked it against 533 jobs we have finished in these categories.
None of it required anything from you.

sheets.title: What stood out
sheets.headline:
Five things stood out.
None of them is a conclusion.

blocks.text: Four observations from the filing, and one thing no filing can show.

items.eyebrow: What you buy is what you sell
items.heading: Your largest indirect line is not overhead. It is inventory.
paras: The biggest expense your filing breaks out apart from people is materials and supplies. In most organizations that line is small and administrative. In yours it is close to the work itself.
items.why: it means the usual assumption about this line is wrong, and we have said so before quoting anything.

items.eyebrow: Your filing names its own suppliers
items.heading: Three relationships are stated in your own words, with amounts.
paras: Part VII Section B asks for the highest-paid contractors, what each was engaged to do and what each was paid. Yours describes the service. Most filings say less.
items.why: it lets us speak about specific arrangements rather than about categories in general.

items.eyebrow: The largest line is not the strongest evidence
items.heading: The category we can say most about is not the one with the most money in it.
paras: Depth of completed work and size of spend are different things, and here they do not point at the same category. We ordered what follows by evidence.
items.why: it is why the second section is not simply the second largest number.

items.eyebrow: One line is a fifth of everything, and we left it alone
items.heading: The single biggest cost after people is reported in a way we will not model.
paras: It combines something we work with something we do not, in one figure, and your return is not required to separate them. We named it and stopped there.
items.why: what we decline to estimate tells you as much as what we estimate.

sheets.title: What stood out
sheets.headline: And one thing no filing can show.

blocks.text: The four above are visible in your return. This one is not, and it is the reason the others are worth asking about.

items.heading: Whether the agreement behind the spend has ever been read by a specialist.
paras: A category can have been bid, renewed, brokered and reviewed, and still carry terms nobody has looked at closely in years. That is not a failure of process. It is what a normal sourcing cycle is not built to catch.
items.why: it is the reason a recent bid is a starting point rather than an answer.

sheets.title: Executive Opportunity Snapshot
sheets.headline:
$82.1M of indirect spend, six categories modelled,
and one is eight times the peer median.

blocks.text: Indirect spend is the recurring operating cost that sits outside your program delivery and outside your payroll — it is the only thing we work. What follows compares the categories your Form 990 names separately against organizations of comparable size and type: a starting point for a question, never a verdict on how you are run.

items.label: Indirect spend, as filed
items.note: Salaries, depreciation and interest are excluded — they are not indirect and not ours to work.

items.label: Named by category
items.note: A further $36.84M sits in lines the filing does not name. ERA works 55 categories; the baseline covers every one that applies.

items.label: Priorities the record can already evidence
items.note: Operating supply, 98th percentile of 2,573 filers; uniforms and linens, 109 completed engagements. Six categories carry a figure.

blocks.text: Evidence depth: four of nine layers carry something for this organization — filed, benchmark, derived and registry. Operating, retrieved, engagement and verified are empty, and are shown as empty rather than filled.

columns.heading: Why operating supply comes first
paras: At 19.4% of revenue against a 2.4% peer median it is roughly eight times, on 2,573 filers. A donated-goods retailer genuinely buys more supply than most nonprofits, so part of that gap is your model rather than your buying — how much is exactly the question. ERA has completed 69 operating-supply engagements at a median of 21%.

columns.heading: Being at the median is not the same as being competitive
paras: The median is drawn from organizations that have mostly never market-tested these categories either. It describes what is normal, not what is available. Of 2,660 completed ERA engagements, 2,649 recovered value — a median of 28% of category spend, and the weakest quarter still returned 14%. Almost none of those clients were outliers on a filing.

sheets.title: Where we would start
sheets.headline: Four lines. Cut it to one if you would rather.

blocks.text: These are the four we would open with. Not because they are the biggest, but because we have finished the most work in them and your filing names them clearly enough to ask a real question.

cells: we would ask how much is resale inventory and how much is consumed supply
we would ask the contract term, and whether the last renewal was tested or rolled over
we would ask the carrier mix, and whether rates were set against today's volume
we would ask what the per-employee fee covers, and what is billed on top
At the median of our finished work, $9.27M a year

blocks.label: Why these four
paras: Why four and not one. One category tells you whether we are useful in that category. Four tells you whether we are useful. You can cut it to one at any point, and most people do.
Why four and not everything. We work fifty-five categories. Your filing lets us see twelve. Starting everywhere is how these things stall.

cells: When was this arrangement last tested against the market, and against what? If the answer is recent, we stop here.
Term, renewal mechanism, service specification, ancillary charges, minimums, and what happens on rollover.
Three months. What is actually being billed against what was agreed. This is where most of it lives.
Someone who works this category repeatedly, not a generalist. They compare your terms against what the market is doing now.
Including keeping your supplier on better terms, which is the most common outcome.
6. You choose, or you do not
Nothing changes without you saying so, and keeping your supplier on better terms is the most common outcome.

paras: A recent market test is useful. We still read the agreement. In this category the value usually sits in the structure rather than the quoted rate — renewal terms, ancillary charges, minimums, replacement practice, service specification, inventory treatment, and what is actually billed. That is why a category can have been reviewed and still be worth an expert second look. The middle half of our finished work here came back between 16% and 42%, and the spread is that wide because the answer depends on the agreement.

sheets.title: The big one
sheets.headline: Operating supply is the largest line, and the least certain.

blocks.text: $37.97M. We are putting it second on purpose, and this page explains why.

columns.text: Most organizations like you spend about 2.4% of revenue on this line. You spend about 19%. Of 2,573 comparable filers, roughly 2,522 spend a smaller share than you do.
You run stores. A donated-goods retailer buys supply the way a retailer does. The gap is very likely your model, not your buying.
How much of it is resale inventory and how much is consumed supply. Your return does not separate them, and the difference changes the answer completely.
So we would ask that first
Before anything else. If most of it is inventory, the part worth working is much smaller and we would tell you so before doing any work.

paras: This is the biggest number in the Report and the one we are least sure about. We would rather say that than lead with it.

sheets.title: A second opinion
sheets.headline:
We are not replacing your process.
We are giving it a second opinion.

blocks.text: Your buyers know the operation. Finance sees the spend. A broker knows its market. A group purchasing agreement gives you negotiated access. Your suppliers know the service. None of that is a problem — it is the environment we expect to find.

cells: Run the process, hold the relationships, know the operation
Depth in one category, and the time to spend on it
Sees the spend, the budget and the variance
Reads the agreement underneath the spend — term, fees, minimums, what is billed on top
The same depth across fifty-five categories
Negotiated access and a floor on price
Tests whether your actual mix and volume are getting the benefit on paper
Knows your operation and keeps it running
An independent read, without having to replace them

blocks.heading: What you get when we find nothing
paras: Confirmation that the incumbent and your process are delivering competitive economics. Evidence that the category was independently reviewed. A record of why no change was recommended.
No unnecessary disruption to a supplier who is doing the job. A baseline to revisit at renewal, or when volume moves. A defensible answer if the category is questioned later.

sheets.title: What happens next
sheets.headline: Answer one question and we will know.

blocks.text: There is no proposal here and no scope of work. The next step is you telling us something the filing could not.

items.heading: You tell us when
paras: For any one of the four lines: when was it last tested, and against what? If the answer is recent, we say so and stop.

items.heading: One contract and three months of invoices
paras: For whichever line you pick. That is the whole of the first data request. Redacted is fine.
items.why: Costs you: an export and an email.

items.heading: We come back with what we found
paras: Category by category, including where we think you are already in good shape. You decide what, if anything, to do.
items.why: Costs you: nothing, and nothing changes without your say-so.

items.heading: Only out of what is actually recovered
paras: We share in the value only when it is actually recovered, after you have it and after it is verified. If we find nothing, there is no fee and no invoice for the work.
Everything in this Report is also online, where you can change any assumption and watch the model move.

sheets.title: The look
sheets.headline:
You may already have this covered.
We are not asking you to assume you do not.

blocks.text: We are asking whether an independent category specialist should validate it.

columns.heading: If your arrangement is strong
paras: Keep it, with confidence, and with an independent read behind the decision.

columns.heading: If there is value left
paras: You see it before anything changes, and you decide whether to act.

blocks.heading: Either way you know more than you knew before.
paras: That is the value of the look. The first one needs one contract and a small sample of invoices, and creates no obligation to change a supplier.

blocks.text: And what your filing could never show us

A Form 990 breaks out only the lines the form asks for. We work fifty-five categories; your filing shows us twelve. Waste, telecoms, packaging, payment processing, maintenance and grounds never reach a return at all. We cannot size them from outside. You can.
